name: Novak Djokovic
bio: The statistical greatest: 24 majors, 428 weeks at No. 1 and the 2024 Olympic gold. Djokovic turned defence into offence with the best return of serve and two-handed backhand the game has seen, plus unmatched flexibility.
strings: Natural gut mains / ALU Power Rough crosses · 59/56 lb

shots.name: The best two-hander ever
shots.why: Technically the cleanest model to copy: compact, balanced, repeatable.
cues: Early shoulder turn; racket set up at shoulder height
Hips drive the swing; both arms extend through contact
Contact well in front and chest height; the top (left) hand does most of the work
Finish high over the right shoulder, chest facing the net

shots.name: The return of serve
shots.why: Djokovic blocks and redirects; a short backswing is something every club player can adopt.
cues: Split step timed with the toss
Tiny takeback; let the server supply the pace
Contact in front, firm wrist, deep to the middle or crosscourt
Recover to the middle before the next ball

shots.name: The redirecting forehand
shots.why: Less extreme than Nadal, more compact than Federer: a reliable middle ground.
cues: Weight on the right leg, then explosive rotation
Contact in front; change direction down the line off a crosscourt ball
Finish across the body or over the shoulder

shots.name: The disguised drop shot
shots.why: Learn the disguise: it must look like a drive until the last moment.
cues: Prepare exactly like a normal groundstroke
Soften the grip and open the face at the last instant
Short, downward-forward cut under the ball
Move forward after it to cover the reply

name: Serena Williams
style: Power baseliner with the best serve in women's tennis
bio: Twenty-three majors across three decades. Serena's serve, the most effective in WTA history, and her inside-out forehand set the power template that the modern women's game still follows.

shots.name: The serve
shots.why: The most copyable elite serve: simple toss, compact motion, full leg drive.
cues: Consistent toss just in front of the head
Trophy position; hips lead the swing
Pronate through contact; land inside the court

shots.name: The inside-out forehand
shots.why: Run around the backhand and attack crosscourt.

shots.name: The down-the-line backhand
shots.why: Flat, early, fearless.
cues: Contact in front; extend down the line

name: Rafael Nadal
bio: The King of Clay. Fourteen Roland Garros titles built on a left-handed forehand with the most revolutions per minute ever measured on tour, relentless defence and a competitive engine that never switched off.
racket: Babolat Pure Aero (100 in², customised to ~340 g)

shots.name: The buggy-whip forehand
shots.why: The low-to-high path is copyable; the lasso finish over the same shoulder is for high, awkward balls only.
cues: Big unit turn with the (right) non-dominant hand across the body
Racket head drops well below the ball with the butt cap pointing at the ball
Legs explode up and the hips rotate violently; contact out in front
Extreme racket-head speed brushing up the ball; finish over the head (lasso) or across the shoulder

shots.name: The deep, looping return
shots.why: Standing deep and hitting heavy, high returns is a smart club strategy.
cues: Stand several metres behind the baseline
Short takeback; let the ball drop into the strike zone
Aim high over the net with heavy topspin, deep to the middle
Recover immediately: the return is only the start of the rally

shots.name: The flat, redirecting backhand
shots.why: A compact, stable two-hander that works for anyone.
cues: Both hands turn the racket back together with the shoulders
Step in on the front foot; knees bent
Contact in front, slightly flatter than the forehand; drive down the line when the ball is short
Finish with both hands over the right shoulder

shots.name: The attacking volley
shots.why: Nadal came to net far more than fans think; his punch volley is textbook.
cues: Split step as the opponent hits
Racket head stays above the wrist; short backswing
Step across with the opposite foot into the ball

name: Steffi Graf
bio: The only player to win the Golden Slam (all four majors plus Olympic gold in 1988). 377 weeks at No. 1, the most ever. Graf ran around everything to hit the "Fräulein Forehand" and sliced the backhand.

shots.name: The Fräulein Forehand
shots.why: Run around the backhand and hit a flat, early forehand with a high finish.
cues: Early preparation with a straight-back takeback
Contact well in front; flat and fast
High finish; recover with crossover steps

shots.name: The backhand slice
shots.why: Graf won 22 majors hitting almost only slice on the backhand. It works.
cues: Use it to set up the forehand

name: Roger Federer
bio: The most complete attacking player of the Open Era. Federer took the ball early, moved like a dancer and could finish points from anywhere with a forehand John McEnroe called "the greatest shot in our sport". Eight Wimbledon titles and 310 weeks at No. 1.
racket: Wilson Pro Staff RF97 Autograph (97 in², 340 g unstrung)
strings: Natural gut mains / Luxilon ALU Power Rough crosses · ~26.5/25 kg

shots.name: The liquid-whip forehand
shots.why: Eastern grip + early contact = the most "natural" pro forehand for club players to copy.
cues: Short, straight takeback with the racket face closed toward the ground
Left hand holds the throat through the unit turn, then points at the ball
Step into the ball on the left foot; contact way out in front, chest height or lower
Relaxed wrist lets the racket head lag and then whip through; finish over the left shoulder

shots.name: The disguised serve
shots.why: Same toss for every serve. You can copy the rhythm and toss even if you cannot copy the disguise.
cues: Platform stance: feet stay apart, no step-up
Toss slightly into the court, identical for flat, slice and kick
Trophy position with the racket tip pointing up and the hitting shoulder dropped
Pronate through contact; land inside the baseline on the left foot

shots.name: The knifing backhand slice
shots.why: The single most useful Federer shot for amateurs: it buys time, changes rhythm and skids low.
cues: Turn fully sideways; racket set up high, above the ball
Step across with the right foot (closed stance)
High-to-low swing with the face slightly open; drive THROUGH the ball, not under it
Left arm swings back for balance; finish with arms spread like wings

shots.name: The topspin one-hander
shots.why: Beautiful but demanding; it needs a strong shoulder turn and precise timing.
cues: Racket back early with the left hand cradling the throat
Weight loads on the back (left) leg, then transfers forward as you step across
Contact well in front with a straight arm; hips stay sideways
Non-hitting arm goes back for counter-balance; finish high

name: Chris Evert
bio: Eighteen majors, seven French Opens and a 125-match clay winning streak. Evert popularised the two-handed backhand and never seemed to miss.
racket: Wilson Chris Evert Autograph (wood) / Wilson Pro Staff

shots.name: The two-handed backhand
shots.why: The original two-hander; compact and flawless.

shots.name: The flat forehand
shots.why: Classic, repeatable, deep.

name: Martina Navratilova
bio: Nine Wimbledon singles titles, 167 singles titles and 59 majors across singles, doubles and mixed. Navratilova brought athletic training and relentless net play to the women's game.

shots.name: The volley
shots.why: The best volleyer in women's history.
cues: Close the net behind the serve

shots.name: The lefty serve-and-volley
shots.why: Serve and move in one motion.
cues: First volley from the service line

name: Pete Sampras
bio: Fourteen majors and six straight year-end No. 1s (1993–98). Sampras owned the 1990s with the best serve in history, a running forehand that ended points and a slam-dunk overhead.
racket: Wilson Pro Staff 6.0 85 (85 in², ~400 g with lead)
strings: Natural gut · very high tension (~75 lb)

shots.name: The greatest serve
shots.why: Copy the rhythm and the full shoulder turn; the second serve kick is the ultimate goal.
cues: Rocking rhythm; toss slightly to the right
Deep knee bend with the back foot sliding up (pinpoint)
Full shoulder rotation; racket drops deep behind the back
Explosive leg drive and pronation; the second serve kicks as hard as the first

shots.name: The running forehand
shots.why: The lesson is balance: hit while moving, then recover.
cues: Plant the outside foot and hit on the move, open stance
Finish and recover with a crossover step

shots.name: The slam dunk
shots.why: Learn the footwork (turn and shuffle back) rather than the leap.
cues: Turn sideways immediately; left hand points at the ball
Racket up early behind the head
Leap, reach high and snap the wrist through contact

name: Björn Borg
bio: Eleven majors by age 25, including five straight Wimbledons and six French Opens. Borg invented the modern topspin baseline game with a Western forehand and a two-handed backhand decades before they became standard.

shots.name: The topspin forehand
shots.why: Heavy spin with huge margin: the safest way to hit hard.
cues: Western grip: palm under the handle
Low racket preparation, knees bent deep
High finish, ball clearing the net by two metres

shots.name: The two-handed passing shot
shots.why: Pass with topspin and dip the ball at the volleyer's feet.
cues: Step across; stay low through contact
Brush up for topspin so the ball dips
Aim crosscourt at a sharp angle or down the line at the feet

name: Monica Seles
bio: Eight majors before her 20th birthday with two hands on both sides and a grunt that announced a new era of power. The 1993 stabbing cut short what might have been the greatest career ever.

shots.name: The two-handed backhand
shots.why: Early, flat and angled.
cues: Take the ball on the rise

shots.name: The attacking return
shots.why: Take the serve on the rise and hit through it.

name: Andre Agassi
bio: The first man to win all four majors on three surfaces in the Open Era plus Olympic gold. Agassi stood on the baseline, took every ball on the rise and returned serve better than anyone before him.
racket: HEAD Radical (Oversize, later Liquidmetal Radical MP)

shots.name: The on-the-rise return
shots.why: Short swing, early contact, aggressive intent: a mindset more than a technique.
cues: Stand on or inside the baseline
Take the ball on the rise; use the server's pace
Hit through the middle to take time away

shots.name: The compact two-hander
shots.why: A perfect model: short, level, repeatable.
cues: Early turn, hands at hip height
Step in; keep the swing level
Contact in front; extend through the target
Short finish, ready for the next ball

name: Ivan Lendl
bio: Eight majors and a record eight straight US Open finals. Lendl professionalised fitness and built the inside-out forehand pattern that modern tennis still runs on.

shots.name: The inside-out forehand
shots.why: Run around the backhand and hit the forehand to the opponent's backhand: the pattern that wins club matches.
cues: Move around the ball with small adjusting steps
Big shoulder turn, contact in front
Aim crosscourt to the opponent's weaker wing

shots.name: The heavy first serve
shots.why: A simple, powerful platform serve.
cues: Land and recover to the baseline

name: Jimmy Connors
bio: 109 titles, the most in ATP history, and five US Open crowns on three surfaces. Connors hit flat with a steel racket and took the ball earlier than anyone of his generation.

shots.name: The flat two-handed backhand
shots.why: A flat, early-contact two-hander that redirects pace.
cues: Step across with the right foot
Drive through; finish toward the target

shots.name: The aggressive return
shots.why: Attack second serves and take the net.

name: Carlos Alcaraz
bio: The youngest men's No. 1 in history and a seven-time major champion by 23, completing the career Grand Slam at the 2026 Australian Open. Alcaraz combines a 100 mph forehand with the best drop shot in the game and fearless net play.
strings: Babolat RPM Blast / natural gut hybrid

shots.name: The disguised drop shot
shots.why: The best drop shot since the 1980s. Study the identical preparation.
cues: Prepare exactly as for a forehand drive
Change the grip and open the face at the last moment
Short cut under the ball with soft hands
Sprint forward to cover the reply

shots.name: The sprinting forehand
shots.why: Enormous racket-head speed from a compact loop.
cues: Finish over the shoulder or lasso on high balls

shots.name: The net attack
shots.why: Alcaraz comes in behind heavy balls; learn when to approach.
cues: Approach behind a deep ball to the weaker wing
Split step at the service line
Volley to the open court or angle it
Close the net for the second volley

name: John McEnroe
bio: The most gifted touch player of his era. McEnroe's side-on left-handed serve, feathered volleys and 1984 season (82–3) are still reference points.

shots.name: The touch volley
shots.why: Soft hands and a short punch: the best volley lesson you can watch.
cues: Racket out in front, head above the wrist
Almost no backswing; meet the ball early
Absorb pace for drop volleys, punch for depth
Move through the volley toward the net

shots.name: The side-on lefty slice serve
shots.why: Learn the slice serve concept; the extreme stance is unique to him.
cues: Back faces the net at the start
Carve around the outside of the ball
Follow it to the net every time

name: Justine Henin
bio: Seven majors and Olympic gold at 1.67 m, with a one-handed backhand McEnroe called the most beautiful shot in tennis and an all-court game that beat the power players.

shots.name: The one-handed backhand
shots.why: Proof that a one-hander works at any size: it is about timing, not strength.
cues: Contact in front with a straight arm

shots.name: The whippy forehand
shots.why: Heavy spin from a light frame: racket-head speed over muscle.

name: Mats Wilander
bio: Won Roland Garros at 17 and three majors in 1988. Wilander out-thought opponents with patience, court construction and a two-hander he could also slice with one hand.

shots.name: The patient two-hander
shots.why: Consistency over power.
cues: Contact in front; topspin for margin

shots.name: The one-handed slice
shots.why: A two-hander who slices with one hand: perfect for variety.
cues: Let go with the top hand
Follow to net when it skids short

name: Venus Williams
bio: Five Wimbledon titles, Olympic singles gold and a 129 mph serve record. Venus's reach and flat power opened the door for her sister.

shots.name: The 129 mph serve
shots.why: Tall players: full extension and a high contact point.

shots.name: The flat two-hander
shots.why: Flat and early.

name: Boris Becker
bio: Wimbledon champion at 17 with the "Boom Boom" serve and diving volleys. Becker's serve-plus-one aggression defined power tennis in the late 1980s.

shots.name: The Boom Boom serve
shots.why: Study the deep knee bend and explosive leg drive.
cues: Rocking weight transfer back then forward
Toss slightly in front; full extension
Explode forward and follow to net

shots.name: The diving volley
shots.why: Do not dive. But do learn to commit fully to the first volley.
cues: Close the net quickly after the serve
Split step as the return is struck
Punch the volley short and angled

name: Iga Świątek
bio: Four Roland Garros titles and the 2025 Wimbledon crown, won 6–0 6–0. Świątek's forehand carries more topspin than almost any woman in history, and her movement on clay is Nadal-like.

shots.name: The heavy topspin forehand
shots.why: The closest thing to Nadal's forehand in the women's game.

shots.name: The early return
shots.why: Aggressive but with spin for margin.

name: Stefan Edberg
bio: The most elegant serve-volleyer ever, with a kick serve that kicked above the shoulder and the best volleys of his generation. Six majors, including the 1992 US Open run of marathon five-setters.

shots.name: The textbook volley
shots.why: If you learn one volley from video, learn this one.
cues: Split step at the service line
Turn the shoulders, not the arm
Step across with the opposite foot
Short punch with a firm wrist; racket head up

shots.name: The kick serve
shots.why: The kick serve is the foundation of a serve-volley game and a safe second serve.
cues: Brush up the back of the ball from 7 to 1 o'clock
Land inside the court already moving to the net

shots.name: The topspin one-hander
shots.why: Smooth and classical.
cues: Contact in front with a straight arm

name: Jannik Sinner
bio: Italy's first men's major champion of the Open Era, with five majors including back-to-back Wimbledon titles in 2025 and 2026. Sinner strikes unusually early off both wings and redirects pace better than anyone on tour.

shots.name: The down-the-line backhand
shots.why: Compact, early and flat: the modern two-hander template.
cues: Unit turn with the hands at chest height
Open stance; load the left leg
Strike early, in front; extend down the line

shots.name: The early-strike forehand
shots.why: Note the timing: contact as the ball rises.
cues: Contact on the rise, flat and deep

shots.name: The attacking return
shots.why: Steps in on second serves and hits deep.

name: Maria Sharapova
bio: Wimbledon champion at 17 and a career Grand Slam by 25. Sharapova hit flat, deep and down the line off both wings and competed harder than anyone.

shots.name: The down-the-line backhand
shots.why: Flat, early, aimed at the lines.

shots.name: The aggressive return
shots.why: Attack every second serve.

name: Aryna Sabalenka
bio: Four majors and the heaviest ball on the WTA. Sabalenka rebuilt her serve in 2022 and became the most consistent force on hard courts, reaching two more Slam finals in 2026.

shots.name: The power forehand
shots.why: Big loop, big legs, big finish.

shots.name: The rebuilt serve
shots.why: An example of fixing a serve with a simpler, rhythmic motion.

name: Naomi Osaka
bio: Four hard-court majors by 23 and the first Asian player to reach No. 1. Osaka's serve and flat forehand end points in three shots.
strings: Yonex Poly Tour Pro / Rexis hybrid

shots.name: The first-strike serve
shots.why: Simple motion, big result.

shots.name: The flat forehand
shots.why: Hits through the court with little margin; add net clearance when you copy it.

name: Andy Murray
bio: Britain's first Wimbledon champion in 77 years, twice Olympic singles champion and the fourth member of the Big Four. Murray's game was built on reading opponents, a world-class return and an unbreakable lob and passing shot.
strings: Luxilon ALU Power / natural gut hybrid · ~58/55 lb

shots.name: The flat two-handed backhand
shots.why: Short, flat and controlled. Pure fundamentals.
cues: Step in with the right foot
Drive through the ball with little topspin; redirect pace
Finish long toward the target before wrapping

shots.name: The chip-and-block return
shots.why: The most practical return for club tennis: get it deep and start the point.
cues: Compact ready position inside the baseline on second serves
Block with a firm wrist; little swing
Chip low with slice against big servers

shots.name: The feathered drop shot
shots.why: Murray used it off both wings; learn it off the backhand first.
cues: Open the face late; soft hands
Cut down and under so it lands short with backspin
Follow it in a step or two

name: Ashleigh Barty
style: All-court with slice and kick serve
bio: Retired as world No. 1 at 25 after winning the 2022 Australian Open. Barty's kick serve and backhand slice were the most effective variety weapons of the modern era.

shots.name: The backhand slice
shots.why: The best modern slice. Learn it to change rhythm.
cues: Knife through with a slightly open face
Follow it forward when it skids

shots.name: The kick serve
shots.why: Kick serve from a 1.66 m player: technique beats height.

name: Elena Rybakina
bio: Wimbledon 2022 champion who became world No. 1 in 2026 after winning both the Australian Open and US Open. Rybakina's serve and flat groundstrokes are the most efficient in the game.

shots.name: The effortless serve
shots.why: Looks slow, measures fast: pure technique and timing.
cues: Full extension with a loose arm

shots.name: The flat forehand
shots.why: Flat and deep with minimal effort.

name: Stan Wawrinka
bio: "Stanimal" won three majors, beating the world No. 1 in each final, with the most powerful one-handed backhand in history and a flat, heavy forehand.
strings: Babolat VS gut / Luxilon ALU Power · ~30 kg

shots.name: The down-the-line hammer
shots.why: Watch for the full shoulder coil; copy the preparation, not the power.
cues: Massive shoulder turn; the back faces the net at the top of the takeback
Weight sits deep on the back leg
Explosive uncoiling; racket accelerates from below the ball
Contact far in front; left arm flies back; finish very high

shots.name: The flat, heavy forehand
shots.why: Penetrating rather than loopy. Good model for players who want to hit through the court.
cues: Compact takeback, racket face slightly closed
Contact in front with a flatter swing path
Finish over the shoulder or around the hip

name: Alexander Zverev
bio: Olympic champion in Tokyo and, after three lost finals, a two-time major champion in 2026 (Roland Garros and US Open). Zverev's 2.0 m frame produces a huge first serve and one of the purest two-handed backhands on tour.

shots.name: The 2.0 m first serve
shots.why: Tall players: copy the high toss and full reach.

shots.name: The pure two-hander
shots.why: As clean as Djokovic's, and easier to see because of the long levers.
cues: High finish over the right shoulder

name: Coco Gauff
style: Athletic counter-puncher with a weapon backhand
bio: US Open champion at 19 and Roland Garros champion in 2025. Gauff is the best mover on tour and owns the most reliable two-handed backhand in the women's game.

shots.name: The two-handed backhand
shots.why: Compact, balanced, repeatable.

shots.name: The first serve
shots.why: Big first serve; a work-in-progress second serve is a useful lesson in itself.

name: Daniil Medvedev
bio: Denied Djokovic the calendar Slam in the 2021 US Open final. Medvedev plays from the back fence, hits unusually flat and serves with a big, disguised action.

shots.name: The flat, laser backhand
shots.why: Ultra flat; learn the compact, level swing but add more margin.
cues: Contact in front, almost no spin

shots.name: The big flat serve
shots.why: Simple, tall, effective.

name: Dominic Thiem
bio: The first man born in the 1990s to win a major (US Open 2020) after two Roland Garros finals. Thiem's one-handed backhand and huge forehand generated extreme racket-head speed.

shots.name: The whipping one-hander
shots.why: Copy the full coil and the explosive hip drive.
cues: Full shoulder turn with a very high takeback
Violent uncoil; contact far in front

shots.name: The heavy forehand
shots.why: Big loop, big spin.

name: Juan Martín del Potro
bio: Beat Nadal and Federer back-to-back to win the 2009 US Open at 20, with the hardest forehand of his era. Wrist surgeries limited him but never his forehand.

shots.name: The flat cannon forehand
shots.why: Flat, early, through the court. Learn the extension through contact.
cues: Step in with the left foot
Contact in front, hit through the ball with a flat path
Long extension toward the target before the finish

shots.name: The survival slice backhand
shots.why: After wrist injuries Delpo rebuilt his backhand around slice. Proof that slice can carry you.
cues: Knife through with an open face

name: Mirra Andreeva
bio: Roland Garros champion in 2026 at 19 and already a top-three player. Andreeva mixes heavy forehands with drop shots and lobs in a way that recalls Hingis.

shots.name: The drop shot
shots.why: Uses it early in rallies to drag opponents forward.

shots.name: The heavy forehand
shots.why: Loopy and heavy with good margin.

name: Gaël Monfils
bio: No major, but the most spectacular athlete of his era: two major semi-finals, the oldest ATP title winner of the 2020s and a highlight reel of dives, tweeners and 2-metre leaps. Included because fans asked.

shots.name: The tweener
shots.why: Learn it for fun on a lob you cannot otherwise reach.
cues: Sprint after the lob, racket low
Let the ball bounce and drop below knee height
Flick the wrist between the legs, racket pointing down
Turn immediately to see where it went

shots.name: The leaping forehand
shots.why: Do not copy the jump. Copy the full shoulder turn.
cues: Contact at the top of the jump

shots.name: The diving volley
shots.why: Pure entertainment.
